description: Hi, this is EchoSphere. I’m a software engineering student who loves data science.  NASA makes amazing visualizations of our planet, but you have to see them to get them. So I’m building the Earth Information Jukebox: a web app that turns real NASA data into music anyone can hear, including blind and low-vision users. Some tracks are chill; some are a bit too hot🔥. My goal is to let anyone hear how our planet is changing. 🎧
summary: Close your eyes. Can you still see our planet changing? For millions of blind and low-vision people, NASA's Earth visualizations are silent pictures. EchoSphere: Hear Our Changing Planet turns them into music. Built for NASA's Earth Information Jukebox challenge, EchoSphere is a free web jukebox where each Earth topic selected plays its own instrument. In "Borneo Haze 2015", a trumpet climbs as Borneo's El Niño fires peak while the rainfall fades and CO₂ hums underneath. Six albums take listeners from local fires to global sea level and the ocean's yearly plankton blooms, because what burns locally echoes globally. We never turn raw colour into noise, EchoSphere reads each visualization's colour legend, or NASA's own data behind it, so every note traces back to a real NASA value. Anyone can go further: build songs in the Studio, hear the weather around any NASA-tracked natural event, or upload an Earth Information Center snapshot and hear it from west to east. Everything works by keyboard and screen reader, never autoplays, and saves as audio to share. EchoSphere doesn't just show climate change. It lets you hear it.
details:
What it does

EchoSphere is a free web jukebox that turns NASA Earth data and Earth Information Center (EIC) visualizations into music, made first for blind and low-vision listeners. Each Earth topic is played by its own instrument, in its own ear, so you can hear how parts of the Earth system move together.

  1. Six albums: Kuching 2015 (Borneo wildfires, Kuching rain and CO₂ during El Niño, weekly Jun–Dec 2015); The Whole Planet 2015 (global fires, CO₂, sea level, monthly 2014–2016); Pacific Drought 2015 (Fiji); South America Floods 2015 (Uruguay River); Black Summer 2019 (New South Wales); and The Ocean Breathes: Diatoms 1998–2012, a solo track of 15 yearly plankton blooms.
  2. Two genres (Orchestra, Modern Band): switchable while playing. Within one song, no two layers use instruments from the same family, so each layer stays easy to pick out.
  3. Mixer with mute and solo per layer, speed control, a timeline chart with a moving playhead and, for some albums, the NASA map frame for each step.
  4. "How to listen" for every album: low, middle and high reference notes, then one note per instrument with what it means. It can be read aloud.
  5. Studio: build your own song from 1–4 layers, choose a genre and an instrument per layer, then share it as a link or keep it in "My songs".
  6. Live events: pick a natural event tracked by NASA EONET (wildfire, storm, volcano and more) and hear NASA POWER weather at that place, 8 weeks before and after.
  7. Any snapshot: upload an EIC picture and hear it west to east. "Find legend automatically" locates the colour bar, reads its numbers and units with in-browser text recognition, and detects linear or logarithmic scales; you can also mark the legend yourself or use a simple colour rule, and choose the map area. Pictures never leave your device.
  8. Save any song as a WAV file.

How it works

  • Get the numbers behind the picture: Where NASA publishes values it use them directly. Where only a visualization exists, Its Python pipeline reads the visualization's colour legend and turns every pixel's colour back into a value. Raw colour is never played as sound.
  • Clean up: Changes smaller than one legend step are merged, so image compression is not heard as music. A Raw/Smoothed switch lets you compare.
  • Values become notes: Higher value means higher pitch, snapped to a pentatonic scale so it stays pleasant. Bigger values are also louder and brighter. Missing data is silence.
  • Every layer is labelled by where its values come from: Decoded from a NASA visualization, NASA values behind a visualization, or NASA data with no visualization.
  • The app is a static website with recorded instrument samples, so it runs in any browser with no login and no server.
  • First time access may result in longer loading process as the available album tuning the value first.

Benefits

  • More accessible science: Opens NASA's Earth visualizations to people who are blind or have low vision, through sound, keyboard control and screen-reader support.
  • A new way to understand data: Listening can reveal patterns, changes and connections between Earth topics that are easy to miss when only looking.
  • Trustworthy: The music comes from real NASA data, and the app shows where each value comes from and what its limits are.
  • Memorable and engaging: Music gives climate data an emotional side, which can help in classrooms, museums and public outreach.
  • Free and easy to use: Runs in any web browser with no account, and anyone can create, save and share their own songs.

What this project wants to achieve

I hope low-vision people, students and the public to explore NASA Earth science by ear. Next steps: test with blind and low-vision listeners, add more EIC visualizations, offer more genres, and work with teachers to use the albums in class.

Tools and languages

JavaScript, HTML and CSS; Tone.js (Web Audio); Tesseract.js (in-browser text recognition for reading legends); Python with NumPy, Pillow and FFmpeg for the data pipeline; GitHub and GitHub Pages for hosting; recorded instrument samples (tonejs-instruments and FluidR3_GM); Claude (Anthropic) as an AI assistant (see Use of AI).

Source code: https://github.com/DanishAsri26/EchoSphere-Hear-Our-Changing-Planet

How AI was used

The idea and every decision are mine (Danish). I worked with Claude (Anthropic) as an AI assistant, like a teammate who helps with the work:

  • Research: finding studies on how people hear data, and finding the right NASA datasets.
  • Writing code: helping build the website and the scripts that turn NASA images into numbers.
  • Checking data: for example, finding the 15 yearly plankton blooms that let us date the diatom video.
  • Writing text: first drafts of this description, the summary and the README, which I then edited.
  • Demo video: the animation was made with AI-written code, and the voice is an AI voice (Kokoro). The video is labelled "AI-GENERATED".
  • Inside the app: the "Find legend automatically" button uses Tesseract.js, a text-reading tool, to read the numbers on a legend. You can check and change what it reads.

What is not AI: all data comes from NASA, and all the music is made by my own code from that data using real recorded instruments.
